svg.text: Глава 5 · Сетевые характеристики и качество обслуживания
Олифер, 7-е изд. · RAG p0131:c01–p0177:c01 · PDF 131–177 · printed 130–176
1 · QoS begins with measurable definitions
SLA = metric + quantitative target + measurement period/method
Delay → OWD · jitter · response time · RTT
Rate → SIR · IIR · PIR · burst size
Reliability → loss ratio · availability · fault tolerance
Statistics → distribution · mean · deviation/CV · quantiles
Active probes create traffic · passive measurement observes real traffic
2 · Application and traffic profile
Stream / CBR-ish → more uniform traffic
Bursty / VBR → silence + peaks
App sensitivity axes → delay/jitter and loss/corruption
Provider view → extensibility · scalability · manageability · compatibility
QoS policy should follow traffic requirements, not one global class
3 · Queueing mechanics
ρ = average arrival intensity / service intensity
As ρ approaches saturation, waiting time grows nonlinearly
Burstiness/CV shifts queue growth earlier
FIFO → simple/no differentiation
Priority → latency preference / starvation risk
Weighted → minimum capacity share per class
4 · Conditioning and feedback
Profiling/policing → drop packets beyond traffic profile
Shaping → buffer/delay excess; may reclassify
Token bucket is named as an algorithm reference in source
Feedback may be endpoint↔endpoint, hop-by-hop, or network→source
Control-loop delay can cause stale reactions / oscillation
Implicit signal example: packet loss in TCP
5 · Reservation and admission control
Before flow: check available unreserved capacity on path
Accepted flow installs reservation/classification state
Weighted queue can implement a reserved share
Priority may be required for very low delay, then profiling is critical
Requested envelope must match actual flow behavior
Exact delay guarantees still require measurement/observed results
6 · Traffic engineering / overprovisioning
Traditional routing may overload shortest path while alternatives idle
Traffic engineering uses topology + capacity + offered load
Goal → balance resources and serve more QoS-constrained flows
Overprovisioning → keep all resources far from overload
Simpler QoS mechanics, higher capacity cost, requires monitoring
Operational reading rule
Do not tune a queue before defining the symptom and measuring the correct metric on the correct time scale.
Do not copy textbook numeric examples into production QoS defaults without SLA, traffic profile and device-specific verification.
No executable CLI is supplied by the chapter.
Questions to Part 1 start at p0178:c01; chapter 6 starts at p0183:c01 · reading state unchanged.
